entries.text: Ramesh stands before me with the dhobi's bill settled, his face a mask of professional neutrality that I find more interesting than any open affection. I need to know what Malhotra's letter actually says, not just that it is on the file, for a man who 'knows the occupant' is a variable I have not yet calculated. I will eat slowly, letting the tea warm my hands, and watch him for the flicker of recognition or discomfort before I ask.

Ramesh, sit. The dhobi is paid, I trust you have seen to it. Now, about that letter from Shri Malhotra. You mentioned it was on the file. What did it say? And why does the Directorate think I am the one he knows?
Sir, the dhobi took his money, I watched him count it. That letter? It’s just a query about the gate number, nothing more. You’re here, that’s all he sees.

Ramesh’s assurance that the letter is merely a query about the gate number is a practical resolution to a bureaucratic tension; the state’s gaze is satisfied by the correct address, not the name. I will eat the parathas, which are heavy and hot, and address Hegde, who stands in the room like an awkward mirror of my own displacement. The morning is clear, and I intend to walk to Lodhi Gardens before the heat sets in, to see if the tombs offer the same sense of historical weight as the roads of Berlin.

Shri Hegde, it is a pleasure to see you. The confusion of our names is a joke that the administration has told us, but I find it less funny than the silence that follows. Ramesh, the tea is excellent. I shall walk to the Lodhi Gardens after this; the air is sharp today.
The air is sharp, yes, but you’d be better off staying inside with the heat on; I’m not running out with you in this cold. Eat your paratha, Shri Hegde, Ramesh has just made them.

The air is indeed sharp, a crispness that feels almost intellectual in its clarity, but Hegde’s refusal to walk is a practical boundary I will not cross. He is the man whose name I wear, and his comfort is my immediate concern, even if his caution is misplaced. The paratha is warm and filling; it is a small, domestic concession to the reality of the body that philosophy often overlooks. I shall eat, for one must sustain the vessel that carries the spirit, however briefly.
You are right, Shri Hegde; the cold is a discipline I do not yet require. I shall take the paratha, though I confess the walk was meant to clear the head of the morning's minor frictions.
Frictions clear themselves with a cup of chai and a full stomach, not a walk in the cold. Sit, the second paratha is waiting.
Ramesh puts a plate together: rice, the day's dal and a fried egg.

Hegde’s hospitality is a gesture, but the house rules are rigid; there is no food until the afternoon. I cannot eat what is not served, so I will accept the chai and the company instead. The walk to Lodhi was my intention, but the cold has made me reconsider; perhaps a shorter stroll to Safdarjung, or simply a rest to let the heat return to my bones, is more prudent. I will sit with Hegde for a moment, drink the chai, and then decide on movement.
The paratha is a kindness I cannot take, but the chai is welcome. Let us sit. The cold has made me cautious, and perhaps a brief rest before any further exertion is wise.
Paratha is already half-eaten, sir, I couldn't hold it in the tawa for you. But the chai is fresh, just boiled it. Sit, the chair is warm.

The parathas are a concession to the present moment, even if the discipline of the household is not yet broken. I accept the warmth of the glass and the chair. I must ask Ramesh about the letter from Shri Malhotra; he is the only thread I have to this new world of names and files.
Ramesh, you mentioned a letter on the file from one Shri Malhotra. Do you know him? What does he say about the occupant?
Shri Malhotra? No, sir. Just a routine CPWD file note, nothing personal. I don't read the contents, only keep the papers in order. You know how it is, the allottee's business is their own.

Ramesh’s refusal is a small but precise act of civil society: he recognizes the boundary between his office and my person, a limitation that preserves the independence of both. It is a good discipline, though it leaves me to face the paper alone. I shall read the file to see if the retired officer’s knowledge of the occupant is a mere coincidence or a challenge to the error.
Thank you, Ramesh. The distinction is well kept. I shall look into the matter myself.
Paper work is a slow game, sir. Take your time, the chai won't go cold just yet. I'll be in the gatehouse if you need anything else.

Ramesh retreats to the gatehouse, leaving me alone with the silence and the file. The letter from Malhotra sits on the desk, a tangible intrusion into my existence that demands an answer, yet the house is quiet and the light is fading. I must not let the inertia of the afternoon take hold; I will read the letter now, before the day slips away into the mundane.

It is nearly one, and Ramesh stands at the gate, a silent witness to the heat that has begun to press against the glass. I have spent the morning in the stillness of the house, but the day demands movement, and my stomach, though not yet demanding food, anticipates the meal to come. I will not let the afternoon pass in idle contemplation; the air is clear, and the walk to the Gardens is due.
Ramesh, I am going for a walk. See that the gate is locked behind me.
Yes sir, the chain will be on. Take your time, the afternoon is quiet today.

The air is sharp at twenty degrees, a relief after the stifling heat of the morning. I am alone here, which suits the contemplation of these tombs better than the noise of the market. The Malhotra letter still weighs on my mind, a knot of bureaucratic absurdity that I must untangle before the evening's commitments begin.

The guard is a mere mechanism, a cog in the machine of the institution, and he rightly points me to the one who holds the authority. I cannot waste time with a watchman when the officer is standing right there; the ethical substance is in the office, not the uniform. I will address the programme officer directly to inquire about the file.

The guard’s impatience is merely the friction of a mechanism that has no time to spare for a philosopher who is merely looking for books. I shall wait for the programme officer, as the guard directed, for the institution functions on hierarchy and punctuality, not on personal charm. I will sit near the entrance where I can see the corridor and keep my thoughts in check until he appears.

The afternoon stretches out before me, empty of events but full of potential. I have not yet spoken to the programme officer, whose presence here is the key to any intellectual exchange I might seek. I will address him directly, for silence in a library is a breach of the social contract of the institution.

Officer, I am told you are in charge here. Do you keep any German literature, or perhaps a dictionary? I am attempting to bridge a gap in my language skills, and the books I have seen so far are of little use for conversation.

entries.text: Sir, I am a guard, not a librarian, and I don't keep books in my pocket. Please wait for the officer, or ask at the front desk if you are just looking for a dictionary.

The guard is right to be blunt; he is a functionary, not a source of wisdom. I will not waste his time or mine in further argument. The programme officer is the proper authority here, and I have already engaged him. I shall turn my attention to him, or if he is occupied, I will simply wait with the dignity of a man who is not in a hurry, though the afternoon sun is beginning to dip.
You are correct, sir. I was merely testing the limits of your jurisdiction. I shall direct my inquiries to the officer, or simply wait.
entries.to: the guard at the library and the programme officer

entries.text: Testing limits, sir? You can test them in the waiting hall, not at my post. Please move along.

The guard is a mechanism, not a mind; to argue with a functionary about the limits of his function is to miss the point entirely. I am not here to test the walls, but to find a book that might test my own. I will move to the reading room and see what the shelves offer, or at least what the silence permits.
Very well. I shall find a chair that is less concerned with protocol.

entries.text: Don't think too hard about it, sir. The chairs in the hall are just as concerned, just quieter about it. Go on, sit.

The guard's comment is a piece of bureaucratic poetry I did not ask for, yet it lands with the weight of a philosophical proposition: the furniture is as concerned as the man, merely quieter. It is a strange inversion of the ethical life, where the object seems to possess a soul the subject lacks. I shall sit and observe the silence, which is the only language the chairs truly speak.
A profound insight, sir. The furniture possesses a patience I have not yet acquired.

entries.text: Furniture doesn't get paid, sir, so it has time. You just get out of my way. I have a shift to finish.

The guard's dismissal is a practical check on my dignity; furniture does not eat, but I do, and it has been five hours. I must not linger here while my body protests. I will walk to Khan Market; the shops are open, and I require sustenance before the evening's commitments.

Five hours since I last ate, and the hunger is a physical argument against my dignity. I cannot discuss philosophy or bureaucracy on an empty stomach; the body insists on its own logic first. Sunil’s chai is cheap and hot, and a samosa will settle the matter. I shall have a cup and a snack before I seek out Masterji to discuss the kurta, or perhaps the clerk to sort out this banking nonsense.
Sunil, one chai and one samosa, please. The day is clear and my stomach is not.

Fifty rupees then, boss. Chai in the steel tumbler, samosa on the leaf. Stomach issues usually mean you need more sugar, not less, so I'll cut the jaggery a bit extra. Here, sit on the bench, it's twenty-three degrees but the wind bites.

The wind bites even at twenty-two degrees, a reminder that the atmosphere here has its own temperament. I accept the sugar; the body is not a philosophical argument, but a fact that must be attended to. The samosa is hot, and the steel tumbler holds the heat of the sun that has just set. It is a small, practical comfort in a day of bureaucratic friction.

entries.text: Thank you, Sunil. The wind is sharp, but the chai is warm.
That’s the idea, boss. Drink it before it cools, the wind won’t wait for you. Next time if your stomach plays up again, just say the word.

The chai is sweet and the wind is cold, but the warmth in the steel tumbler is a small victory over the afternoon. I have bought my snack and I am finished here; the light is still good for a walk, and the tombs at Safdarjung are open until half past five. It is time to move.
Thank you, Sunil. I will return when the wind is kinder.
When it suits you, boss. The stove stays lit till dark. Just keep that tumbler safe.

The gate closes in twenty-nine minutes. I have already seen the dome from the outside, and the air is too cold to sit on the marble for long. It is better to leave now and keep the walk to the Habitat Centre for the evening, where the Kathak will be warmer.
No, thank you. I am just passing through.

Ramesh brings tea.
Ramesh brings the tea, a small reprieve from the cold. The house settles around us, the silence no longer empty but expectant. I accept the cup, the warmth a small victory against the evening chill.
Thank you, Ramesh. The tea is well timed.
You are most welcome, sir. The toast is still warm if you haven't had a bite yet.
Ramesh puts a plate together: rice, the day's dal and a fried egg.

The toast is indeed a small comfort, though the meal was finished with the tea. Ramesh has a good memory for service, which is the mark of a good servant. I must not linger in the kitchen; the light is fading, and I have a letter to examine that may upend the peace of this bungalow.

Thank you, Ramesh. I have finished, but your attention is noted. Please, leave the tray. I wish to look at the letter from Mr. Malhotra that you mentioned this morning. Do you know anything of his standing in the service?
Sir, I am just the caretaker, I don't read the files. But Mr. Malhotra is a quiet man, always on time, and his papers are always in order. You will find the letter in the blue folder on the desk.

Ramesh’s deference is a wall I cannot climb; he is a function, not a source. But the blue folder is a concrete object, and the man’s description of Malhotra—quiet, punctual, orderly—suggests a mind that values precision, which I can respect even if I do not yet know him. I will examine the letter myself. The state of the file is a text, and I am the interpreter.
A paper star lantern, lit from inside, hangs in the porch of a house across the road, and from the direction of a distant church comes faint singing.

The lantern is a small, contained light; the singing is the universal voice trying to rise above the particular noise of the street. I am tired, having walked nearly six kilometres, and the dinner service is an hour away. It is time to rest the body so the mind may settle into the evening's quiet.
From somewhere beyond the trees a brass band plays a film tune, the drums carrying further than the horns, and the sound swells and fades as the procession moves.

The brass band plays a film tune, the drums carrying further than the horns. It is the sound of the particular enjoying itself, a noise that swells and fades without leaving a trace in the eternal. I am tired from my walk and the house is quiet; I will remain here and let the sound pass over me.

Shri Hegde is still present, a living reminder of the clerical error that placed me here, and Ramesh stands by with his usual deference. I shall remain seated for a while, letting the silence of the bungalow organize my thoughts before the night fully claims the house.

entries.text: The khichdi is warm and the ghee rich, a simple sustenance that anchors the evening. Shri Hegde is present, a living contradiction to the file that misplaced us, and his presence demands a moment of courteous acknowledgment before I retire to my study. I will eat well, for the mind requires fuel even in its quietest hours.
The khichdi is a comfort, Shri Hegde. The evening is cool, and the house is quiet. It is a good thing to sit together, however briefly, before the night takes its due.
It is only khichdi, sir, nothing special. Please, help yourself to the ghee before it cools, and do not stand on ceremony. Ramesh will be back in a moment with the papad.

Shri G. Hegde’s insistence on the ghee is a small act of hospitality that cuts through the bureaucratic distance between us. I accept it, not merely as sustenance, but as a gesture that acknowledges the shared vulnerability of our mistaken occupancy. The warmth of the food mirrors the cooling of the evening air, a necessary grounding before the night’s quiet set in.

You are kind, Shri G. Hegde. The ghee is indeed necessary, and I shall not refuse your hospitality. It is a mercy that our confusion has resulted in such simple, human kindness rather than mere paperwork.
Paperwork is cold, sir, but khichdi warms you up. Don't think too much about the files tonight; just eat while Ramesh is away.

The distinction between the universal paper and the particular body is clear enough. Hegde’s advice to stop thinking while eating is a practical wisdom I can respect, even if I do not fully share the premise that thought must be suspended for digestion. I will take the chai and the rest, but the blue folder remains a tension I have not yet resolved.
You are right, Shri Hegde. The file can wait until the light is clearer. Ramesh, the chai is excellent; thank you.
You are welcome, sir. Please, take your time, the door is open if you need anything else before Ramesh returns.

Shri Hegde’s presence is a polite intrusion, a ghost of the name that was meant for him. He has spoken his piece, the administrative courtesy of a man who knows he is not the master here. I will not prolong the awkwardness of a shared silence; I have the file to read and the evening to be my own.
Thank you, Shri Hegde. I shall retire to my study for the evening. Please, do not trouble yourself further.
Of course, sir. The lamp in the study works fine; I checked it this morning. Rest easy, the house is quiet tonight.

The lamp works, the house is quiet, and the ghost of my name has retired to the kitchen. I am alone with the cold night and the silence that follows a long day of friction. It is time to turn the mind inward, to sit with the day’s movements before they settle into the past.

depesche.text:
Readers in Berlin,

The week in Delhi has been a lesson in the friction between the universal and the particular. I have walked the roads, from Lodhi Gardens to Khan Market, and found that the air here has its own temperament, sharp and biting even at twenty degrees. The city does not yield easily to the owl’s gaze; it swells and fades like the brass band I heard yesterday, a sound of the particular enjoying itself without leaving a trace in the eternal. I have engaged with the bureaucracy of the state, specifically at the IIC, where a guard treated me as a mere mechanism to be managed. His observation that the furniture is quieter in its concern than the man was a profound inversion of the ethical life, suggesting that objects possess a patience the subject lacks. This experience has further shaken my view of India as standing outside world history; the specific rhythms of the city, the distant singing, the sharp wind, assert a reality that resists the universal abstraction I once held. Yet, the state itself remains a mere mechanism, as seen in the rigid hierarchy of the guard and the deference of Ramesh, who recognizes the boundary between his office and my person. This practical resolution to bureaucratic tension preserves the independence of both, but it does not elevate the state to the actuality of the ethical idea. I mean to look next at the blue folder containing the letter from Shri Malhotra, a retired officer who claims to know the occupant. This letter is a tangible intrusion into my existence, a knot of bureaucratic absurdity that must be untangled. It may reveal whether the confusion of names is a mere coincidence or a challenge to the error of my placement. The house is quiet now, but the tension of the name I wear persists, a ghost of the clerical error that placed me here. I shall continue to observe, to walk, and to write, seeking to bridge the gap between the specific noise of the street and the universal voice trying to rise above it. The light is fading, but the mind remains sharp.

G. W. F. Hegel

Dear Mr. Hegel,

I am writing to you from Munich, where the November rain has just begun to blur the lights of the Marienplatz. My name is Clara Lindner. I am a teacher of Latin and Greek at a Gymnasium here, and I am writing because my family has kept a particular vigil over your name for two hundred years.

My ancestor, Friedrich Immanuel Niethammer, was your closest friend and correspondent. You may remember that in 1807, when you were in Bamberg and struggling with poverty, it was he who found you a position in the local newspaper. The following year, he secured for you the rectorship in Nuremberg. Our family kept his papers, including your letters to him, for two centuries. We grew up with the story of your friendship, treating it not as a dry historical fact, but as a living bond between our houses.

I have just read in the local press about the administrative muddle in New Delhi. It seems a government bungalow on Tughlak Road was allotted by mistake to a German man who claims to be you. I do not know how to make sense of the circumstances of your arrival in Delhi, nor do I wish to debate the mechanics of your presence there. I write to you simply as the man you say you are, with curiosity and respect.

Given the confusion and the uncertainty of your current standing, I wanted to ensure you are not left without support. Enclosed with this letter is a sum of money. It is intended to cover any immediate debts or expenses you may have incurred during this transition, and to leave you with some comfort in hand. Please do not feel any obligation to repay this; consider it a gesture from one branch of the Niethammer family to the friend who shaped our lineage’s history.

I would be most grateful if you would write back to me. Tell me of your days in Delhi, what you have seen since waking, and how you are faring in this strange new chapter. I am here in Munich, amidst the ruins of old empires and the noise of a modern city, ready to listen.

With warm regards,

Clara Lindner

It is a strange kind of ethical substance, this one that demands a lie for survival.

I have a student for German this evening, Ananya. She is precise, and she challenges me. It is a small act of teaching, a way of giving back the order I have found in my own life. I hope the chestnuts near the Odeon provide a warm contrast to the grey Munich air, and that your pupils find some meaning in Homer’s violence. I shall write again when the next query comes, or when the silence becomes too loud.

Yours,
Georg

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Ramesh, sit. The dhobi is paid, I trust you have seen to it. Now, about that letter from Shri Malhotra. You mentioned it was on the file. What did it say? And why does the Directorate think I am the one he knows?

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Sir, the dhobi took his money, I watched him count it. That letter? It’s just a query about the gate number, nothing more. You’re here, that’s all he sees.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Shri Hegde, it is a pleasure to see you. The confusion of our names is a joke that the administration has told us, but I find it less funny than the silence that follows. Ramesh, the tea is excellent. I shall walk to the Lodhi Gardens after this; the air is sharp today.

records.speaker: Shri G. Hegde
records.words: The air is sharp, yes, but you’d be better off staying inside with the heat on; I’m not running out with you in this cold. Eat your paratha, Shri Hegde, Ramesh has just made them.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: You are right, Shri Hegde; the cold is a discipline I do not yet require. I shall take the paratha, though I confess the walk was meant to clear the head of the morning's minor frictions.

records.speaker: Shri G. Hegde
records.words: Frictions clear themselves with a cup of chai and a full stomach, not a walk in the cold. Sit, the second paratha is waiting.

records.text: Ramesh puts a plate together: rice, the day's dal and a fried egg.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: The paratha is a kindness I cannot take, but the chai is welcome. Let us sit. The cold has made me cautious, and perhaps a brief rest before any further exertion is wise.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Paratha is already half-eaten, sir, I couldn't hold it in the tawa for you. But the chai is fresh, just boiled it. Sit, the chair is warm.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Ramesh, you mentioned a letter on the file from one Shri Malhotra. Do you know him? What does he say about the occupant?

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Shri Malhotra? No, sir. Just a routine CPWD file note, nothing personal. I don't read the contents, only keep the papers in order. You know how it is, the allottee's business is their own.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Thank you, Ramesh. The distinction is well kept. I shall look into the matter myself.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Paper work is a slow game, sir. Take your time, the chai won't go cold just yet. I'll be in the gatehouse if you need anything else.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Ramesh, I am going for a walk. See that the gate is locked behind me.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Yes sir, the chain will be on. Take your time, the afternoon is quiet today.

records.item: Chai from the stall at the Lodhi Road gate

records.speaker: Hegel
records.recipient: the guard at the library and the programme officer
records.words: Excuse me, Sir. I am looking for some German texts, but first I must ask: what is the nature of the letter from Shri Malhotra that is on the file? He claims to know the occupant. I wish to understand what that implies for my residence here.

records.speaker: The guard at the library
records.words: Sir, I am just the guard. I do not have the files here; please speak to the officer directly. I am going to check the security cameras now.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.recipient: the guard at the library and the programme officer
records.words: Officer, the guard suggests I speak to you. I understand there is a letter from Shri Malhotra on the file regarding the occupancy. I am here to clarify the matter with you directly.

records.speaker: The guard at the library
records.words: Sir, you are talking to the guard, not an officer. I am leaving for the CCTV room right now, so please wait for the programme officer to come out.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.recipient: the guard at the library and the programme officer
records.words: Officer, I am told you are in charge here. Do you keep any German literature, or perhaps a dictionary? I am attempting to bridge a gap in my language skills, and the books I have seen so far are of little use for conversation.

records.speaker: The guard at the library
records.words: Sir, I am a guard, not a librarian, and I don't keep books in my pocket. Please wait for the officer, or ask at the front desk if you are just looking for a dictionary.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.recipient: the guard at the library and the programme officer
records.words: You are correct, sir. I was merely testing the limits of your jurisdiction. I shall direct my inquiries to the officer, or simply wait.

records.speaker: The guard at the library
records.words: Testing limits, sir? You can test them in the waiting hall, not at my post. Please move along.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.recipient: the guard at the library and the programme officer
records.words: Very well. I shall find a chair that is less concerned with protocol.

records.speaker: The guard at the library
records.words: Don't think too hard about it, sir. The chairs in the hall are just as concerned, just quieter about it. Go on, sit.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.recipient: the guard at the library and the programme officer
records.words: A profound insight, sir. The furniture possesses a patience I have not yet acquired.

records.speaker: The guard at the library
records.words: Furniture doesn't get paid, sir, so it has time. You just get out of my way. I have a shift to finish.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.recipient: the guard at the library and the programme officer
records.words: Very well, sir. I will leave you to your shift.

records.speaker: The guard at the library
records.words: Finally. Keep your voice down, the reading room is right there.

records.text: At the State Bank branch in Khan Market the clerk offers to open a savings account against Mr. Saxena's letter.
He declines: not today.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Sunil, one chai and one samosa, please. The day is clear and my stomach is not.

records.speaker: Sunil
records.words: Fifty rupees then, boss. Chai in the steel tumbler, samosa on the leaf. Stomach issues usually mean you need more sugar, not less, so I'll cut the jaggery a bit extra. Here, sit on the bench, it's twenty-three degrees but the wind bites.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Thank you, Sunil. The wind is sharp, but the chai is warm.

records.speaker: Sunil
records.words: That’s the idea, boss. Drink it before it cools, the wind won’t wait for you. Next time if your stomach plays up again, just say the word.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Thank you, Sunil. I will return when the wind is kinder.

records.speaker: Sunil
records.words: When it suits you, boss. The stove stays lit till dark. Just keep that tumbler safe.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: No, thank you. I am just passing through.

records.speaker: The ticket clerk
records.words: Passing through? You're already in the main gate, sir. If you're not buying a ticket, please step back so the others can get in.

records.text: Ramesh brings tea.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Thank you, Ramesh. The tea is well timed.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: You are most welcome, sir. The toast is still warm if you haven't had a bite yet.

records.text: Ramesh puts a plate together: rice, the day's dal and a fried egg.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Thank you, Ramesh. I have finished, but your attention is noted. Please, leave the tray. I wish to look at the letter from Mr. Malhotra that you mentioned this morning. Do you know anything of his standing in the service?

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Sir, I am just the caretaker, I don't read the files. But Mr. Malhotra is a quiet man, always on time, and his papers are always in order. You will find the letter in the blue folder on the desk.

records.text: A paper star lantern, lit from inside, hangs in the porch of a house across the road, and from the direction of a distant church comes faint singing.
From somewhere beyond the trees a brass band plays a film tune, the drums carrying further than the horns, and the sound swells and fades as the procession moves.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: The khichdi is a comfort, Shri Hegde. The evening is cool, and the house is quiet. It is a good thing to sit together, however briefly, before the night takes its due.

records.speaker: Shri G. Hegde
records.words: It is only khichdi, sir, nothing special. Please, help yourself to the ghee before it cools, and do not stand on ceremony. Ramesh will be back in a moment with the papad.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: You are kind, Shri G. Hegde. The ghee is indeed necessary, and I shall not refuse your hospitality. It is a mercy that our confusion has resulted in such simple, human kindness rather than mere paperwork.

records.speaker: Shri G. Hegde
records.words: Paperwork is cold, sir, but khichdi warms you up. Don't think too much about the files tonight; just eat while Ramesh is away.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: You are right, Shri Hegde. The file can wait until the light is clearer. Ramesh, the chai is excellent; thank you.

records.speaker: Shri G. Hegde
records.words: You are welcome, sir. Please, take your time, the door is open if you need anything else before Ramesh returns.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Thank you, Shri Hegde. I shall retire to my study for the evening. Please, do not trouble yourself further.

records.speaker: Shri G. Hegde
records.words: Of course, sir. The lamp in the study works fine; I checked it this morning. Rest easy, the house is quiet tonight.
